intent: A clockmaker's tour of the planet: the table, then the two islands at either end of a French day, then the giant that refused to split its clock.

v04.text: France. Not the hexagon on the map, but its islands around the world: 12 time zones.

v05.text: Russia stretches 11 across a single landmass. The United States, with its islands, also 11. France: 12.

v06.text: Its clocks run from Tahiti, at UTC minus 10, to Wallis and Futuna, at plus 12: a gap of 22 hours.

v07.text: And China, nearly as wide as the United States, picked a single clock: Beijing time, everywhere.

research.topic: Country with the most time zones: France, 12 (metropolitan France plus overseas departments and territories from French Polynesia at UTC−10 to Wallis and Futuna at UTC+12); Russia 11 (UTC+2 Kaliningrad to UTC+12 Kamchatka); United States 11 including territories (UTC−12 Baker Island to UTC+10 Guam, 6 across the 50 states); China spans about five geographic zones but uses one official time (UTC+8).

myths.myth: Russia has the most time zones because it is the widest country.
myths.reality: Russia has 11 across one landmass; France reaches 12 through overseas territories from Tahiti to Wallis and Futuna.

landscape.our_gap: Feed clips say 'France 12' as a one-liner; nobody draws the table, pins the two islands at either end of the French day and sets China's single clock against them on a moving map.

tad_france.title: Time zones in France
tad_france.notes: France and its dependencies use 12 time zones, from UTC−10 (Tahiti, French Polynesia) to UTC+12 (Wallis and Futuna); Paris UTC+1/+2

tad_russia.title: Time zones in Russia
tad_russia.notes: Russia uses 11 time zones, UTC+2 (Kaliningrad) to UTC+12 (Kamchatka)

tad_usa.title: Time zones in the United States
tad_usa.notes: the USA and its dependencies use 11 time zones (UTC−12 to UTC+10); 6 across the 50 states

tad_china.title: Time zones in China
tad_china.notes: China uses a single time zone, China Standard Time UTC+8, although it spans five geographic zones
